questions.question: Under an $(s,S)$ inventory policy with i.i.d. period demands $D$, the hitting-time recursion uses $T(s,x)$ for an inventory position $x>s$. What does $T(s,x)$ denote?
options: The expected total demand that occurs until the inventory position first lies at or below $s$, starting from $x$.
The expected number of periods with positive demand until the position first lies at or below $s$, starting from $x$.
The expected number of periods until the inventory position first lies at or below $s$, starting from $x$.
The probability that the inventory position, starting from $x$, lies at or below $s$ after exactly one period.

questions.question: For the inventory position under an $(s,S)$ policy with i.i.d. period demand $D$, the expected hitting time satisfies $T(s,x)=1+\mathbb{E}[T(s,x-D)]$ for $x>s$. What does the term $1$ account for?
options: The one period that passes before the next position $x-D$ is reached, whatever the demand turns out to be.
The single replenishment order that is placed once the position enters the set $\{x\colon x\leq s\}$.
The extra period caused by a zero demand, which occurs with probability $f_0=\mathbb{P}(D=0)$.
The boundary value $T(s,s)=1$, because one more review is needed once the position is at $s$.

questions.question: With $f_k=\mathbb{P}(D=k)$ for the period demand $D$ under an $(s,S)$ policy, the recursion $T(s,x)=1+\sum_{k\geq0}f_kT(s,x-k)$ for $x>s$ contains $T(s,x)$ on both sides. Why?
options: Memoization requires every value to be expressed through itself before it can be stored in the cache.
A period with zero demand, which has probability $f_0$, leaves the inventory position at $x$ itself.
After the position falls to $s$ or below, an order raises it again, so the process can come back to $x$.
First-step conditioning always puts the unknown on both sides, also when the demand is never zero.

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$, the expected time to empty the system starting from $q$ jobs is $T(q)=q\,\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$. Which reading of this formula is correct?
options: Each of the $q$ jobs waits on average $\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$ in the queue, and $T(q)$ adds up these $q$ waiting times.
The $q$ services take $q\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, and the factor $1/(1-\rho)$ adds the idle time of the server between them.
The $q$ services take $q\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, and each service is repeated with probability $\rho$, as with a self-loop.
Clearing one job together with all jobs that arrive meanwhile takes a mean busy period $\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$, once per job.

questions.question: For the inventory position under an $(s,S)$ policy with period demand pmf $f_k=\mathbb{P}(D=k)$, the hitting-time recursion divides by $1-f_0$ and assumes $f_0<1$. What is the expected hitting time $T(s,x)$, $x>s$, if $f_0=1$?
options: It equals $1$, because exactly one period is counted before the position is checked again.
It is still finite; the condition $f_0<1$ only avoids a division by zero in the formula.
It is infinite, because the demand is always zero and the position stays at $x$ for ever.
It equals $x-s$, because the position then falls by exactly one unit in every period.

questions.question: Under an $(s,S)$ policy, period demands are i.i.d. with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=f_0=0.2$. What is the expected number of periods $T(s,s+1)$ until the inventory position, starting at $s+1$, first lies at or below $s$?

In an $M/G/1$ queue, jobs arrive at rate $\lambda=3$ per hour and the mean service time is $\mathbb{E}[S]=0.2$ hours. Starting with $q=4$ jobs in the system, what is the expected time $T(4)$ until the system is empty for the first time?
options: $0.8$ hours
$1.28$ hours
$1.33$ hours
$2$ hours

questions.question: In an $M/M/1$ queue with arrival rate $\lambda=1$ and service rate $\mu=3$, let $T(q)$ be the expected time until the system is first empty, starting from $q$ jobs. Which first-step equation holds for $q\geq1$?

An $(s,S)$ policy has $s=10$, $S=15$, mean period demand $\mathbb{E}[D]=2$ and ordering cost $K=58$ per order. The hitting-time recursion gives the expected cycle length $T(s,S)=2.9$ periods. What is the long-run ordering cost per period?

Under an $(s,S)$ policy with $s=2$, each period's demand is $0$ or $1$ unit, with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each. Which pair gives the expected numbers of periods $T(2,2)$ and $T(2,3)$ until the inventory position first lies at or below $2$?

A memoized recursive function computes the $(s,S)$ hitting time as $T(x)=0$ for $x\leq s$ and $T(x)=1+\sum_{d\geq0}f_dT(x-d)$ for $x>s$, keeping the term $d=0$, with $f_0>0$. What happens when it is called with $x=s+1$?
options: It returns the correct value, because the cache stores the first call and reuses it for the inner call.
It returns $1$, because the unfinished inner call $T(s+1)$ is read from the cache as the value $0$.
It is correct for $x=s+1$ and only fails for larger $x$, where two levels above the set are needed.
It does not return a value, because computing $T(s+1)$ calls $T(s+1)$ itself before that value is in the cache.

questions.question: For $x>s$ the inventory hitting time satisfies $T(s,x)=\big(1+\sum_{k\geq1}f_kT(s,x-k)\big)/(1-f_0)$, with $T(s,x)=0$ for $x\leq s$ and $f_k=\mathbb{P}(D=k)$. Why can all values be computed by a single loop over $x=s+1,s+2,\dots$?
options: Every term on the right uses a position below $x$, which lies in the set or was computed earlier in the loop.
The loop works only for bounded demand; unbounded demand would need values that are not known yet.
Dividing by $1-f_0$ makes each update contracting, so the loop converges from any starting values.
The loop follows the inventory position in time, so each value uses states the process has already visited.

questions.question: Under an $(s,S)$ policy with demand pmf $f_k$, each period that starts at a position $x>s$ costs $c(x)$, and entering the set $\{x\colon x\leq s\}$ costs $K$ once. How should the recursion for $T(s,x)$ be changed to give the expected cost $V(x)$ until the set is entered?
options: Replace $1$ by $c(x)$ and the boundary $0$ by $K$, but drop the factor $1/(1-f_0)$, which only counts idle time.
Take $V(x)=c(x)\,T(s,x)+K$, since each period until the set is entered costs $c(x)$.
Replace $1$ by $c(x)$ and the boundary $0$ by $K$, and keep the division by $1-f_0$.
Replace $1$ by the next position's cost $\mathbb{E}[c(x-D)]$ and the boundary $0$ by $K$.

questions.question: Under an $(s,S)$ policy with $s=2$, each period's demand is $0$ units with probability $0.4$ and $1$ unit with probability $0.6$. What is the expected number of periods $T(2,5)$ until the inventory position, starting at $5$, first lies at or below $2$?
options: $3$ periods
$7.5$ periods
$\tfrac{5}{3}$ periods
$5$ periods

questions.question: Under an $(s,S)$ policy with $s=3$, each period's demand is $1$ unit with probability $0.4$ and $2$ units with probability $0.6$. Starting at position $4$, compare the expected time to reach the set $\{x\colon x\leq3\}$ with that to reach the set $\{3\}$. Which pair is correct?
options: $1$ period for $\{x\colon x\leq3\}$; infinite for $\{3\}$, as the position may jump to $2$ and never return.
$1$ period for either set, because every demand moves the position below $4$ in the first period.
$1$ period for $\{x\colon x\leq3\}$; $2.5$ periods for $\{3\}$, waiting for a demand of exactly one.
$0.625$ periods for $\{x\colon x\leq3\}$, which is $(4-3)/\mathbb{E}[D]$; $1$ period for $\{3\}$.

questions.question: In an $M/G/1$ queue with $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$, let $Y$ be the number of arrivals during one service, so $\mathbb{E}[Y]=\rho$. The expected time to empty satisfies $T(q)=\mathbb{E}[S]+\mathbb{E}[T(q+Y-1)]$ for $q\geq1$, with $T(0)=0$. What role does $T(0)=0$ play?
options: None: the step equation alone already determines every $T(q)$ once $\rho<1$ is given.
It fixes the slope: the step equation allows any slope, and $T(0)=0$ selects $\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)$.
Every $T(q)=q\,\mathbb{E}[S]/(1-\rho)+c$ satisfies the step equation; $T(0)=0$ selects $c=0$.
It is the wrong boundary: the last job needs one service, so it should be $T(1)=\mathbb{E}[S]$.

questions.question: The recursion $T(s,x)=1+\mathbb{E}[T(s,x-D)]$ for an $(s,S)$ inventory position treats period demands as i.i.d. Suppose instead that a high-demand period tends to be followed by another high-demand period. What goes wrong with a recursion in $x$ alone?
options: Nothing: the law of total expectation holds for any demand process, so the recursion in $x$ stays valid.
The next demand's law depends on the last demand, so the expected time from $x$ is not a function of $x$ alone.
Only $f_0$ changes: using the conditional probability of zero demand instead repairs the recursion in $x$.
Nothing, as long as $f_0<1$: the set is then still reached, and the recursion in $x$ stays valid.

questions.question: In an $M/M/1$ queue with arrival rate $\lambda=2$ and service rate $\mu=5$ per hour, let $T(q)$ be the expected time to empty the system from $q$ jobs, with $T(0)=0$. Write the first-step equation for $q\geq1$ and try $T(q)=aq$. Which value of $a$ (in hours) solves it?

Let $T(0,x)$ be the expected hitting time, in periods, of the set $\{x\colon x\leq0\}$ for an $(s,S)$ inventory position with $s=0$ and demand pmf $f_0=0.2$, $f_1=0.4$, $f_2=0.4$. Building the values upwards from the boundary, which value does $T(0,3)$ take?
